title: Data Center & Networking Daily Briefing
description: AI fabrics and enterprise networking, data center capacity, power and cooling, and AI storage.
readFirst: Covers Nov. 17–27. New: Tom's Hardware reported Nov. 26 that electronics makers have set up procurement war rooms for DRAM, and that SK hynix has called 2027 the worst year of the shortage. No new networking-product or power announcement dated Nov. 26–27 was opened. WWT's Nov. 24 note on PowerStoreOS 5.1 remains on the WWT page. The Army's request for power and data-center leases at nine installations remains on the Army page.

items.headline: Nvidia and Cisco plan a USFP optical module for AI factory networks
items.summary: NVIDIA said Nov. 17 that it plans, with Cisco, a new optical-module form factor called USFP, designed to increase bandwidth density and power efficiency for next-generation AI factory networks. The announcement was part of NVIDIA's fiscal 2027 third-quarter release. That release also said Cisco, Google, Meta, Microsoft, and Visionbay are joining other technology leaders advancing infrastructure for Vera Rubin. NVIDIA did not publish a ship date for USFP in the release.

items.headline: Tom's Hardware: lenders back a $43 billion SpaceX loan for Nvidia chips
items.summary: Tom's Hardware reported Nov. 22 that Elon Musk is borrowing $43 billion to finance SpaceX's acquisition of Nvidia AI chips and is using the semiconductors as collateral. Tom's Hardware said Ars Technica reported that lenders worry the chips could be placed in a planned orbital data center and would then be difficult to reclaim in a default. Tom's Hardware said SpaceX said the collateralized chips will be deployed only on Earth, and that it is unclear whether that limit is written into the signed debt instrument. Tom's Hardware said the Project Saturn loan is structured like an aircraft lease, with a leasing company buying the chips, rather than as a typical loan, and that Musk has also described a planned $24 billion gas-powered AI supercomputer in Starbase, Texas.

items.headline: Tom's Hardware: Trump says he wants to stop U.S. firms building data centers abroad
items.summary: Tom's Hardware reported Nov. 21, citing Axios, that President Donald Trump said he wants to prevent U.S. companies from building data centers in other countries or to charge a "tremendous tax" if they do, and that he said he has not discussed the idea with his cabinet or advisers. Tom's Hardware quoted Trump saying the companies are making so much money they do not know what to do with it, and that "we're not allowing data centers to go into other countries because China will take all of them." Tom's Hardware said one reason under discussion is Chinese labs sending work to overseas data centers that use chips barred from export to China, including Nvidia Blackwell and the upcoming Vera Rubin. Tom's Hardware said data-center moratoriums in the United States have passed 500, and that only Congress can impose a tax.

items.headline: Tom's Hardware: AI server prices are rising up to 45 percent after contracts are signed
items.summary: Tom's Hardware reported Nov. 23, citing the Financial Times, that trading and financial-services firms are seeing price increases of up to 45 percent on data-center servers after contracts were signed, often months earlier. Tom's Hardware said one unnamed person described increases of 25, 30, and 45 percent, and that another said the firm had not turned the higher price down because the compute is valuable. Tom's Hardware said the Financial Times asked whether the contracts barred price changes and that none of the companies confirmed or denied such a clause. Tom's Hardware said the Financial Times attributed the increases to memory prices, with GPU servers up 20 to 30 percent and memory-heavy CPU nodes doubled or tripled.

items.headline: Fortune: OpenAI names TensorWave for 457 megawatts of AMD capacity
items.summary: Fortune reported Nov. 17 that OpenAI named TensorWave as the first neocloud provider tied to a compute deal OpenAI signed with AMD in October for 6 gigawatts of capacity. Fortune said TensorWave will provide 457 megawatts across multiple U.S. data center sites, and that a TensorWave spokesperson called it the company's largest deployment and said the company will need to roughly triple its staff. Fortune said that capacity is expected in the first half of 2027, with the full deployment expected by early 2028, and that the first gigawatt of the AMD deal is set to come online in the second half of this year.

items.headline: Tom's Hardware: the IEA is tracking 93 AI factories headed toward 50 gigawatts
items.summary: Tom's Hardware reported Nov. 19 that the International Energy Agency's World Energy Outlook 2026 counts 120 gigawatts of data-center capacity worldwide today and expects another 120 gigawatts to be completed by the end of the decade, with 75 percent of that addition dedicated to artificial intelligence. Tom's Hardware said the agency is tracking 93 large AI factories under construction or expansion and estimates those sites grew from under 2 gigawatts to 17 gigawatts in two years, with 50 gigawatts expected when they are finished, which Tom's Hardware compared to adding a second Great Britain of power demand. The agency said its analysis does not yet show a clear relationship between data-center growth and higher electricity prices. Tom's Hardware said the outlook expects coal- and natural-gas emissions from data centers to rise 70 percent by 2030.

items.headline: Tom's Hardware: a SpaceXAI site spilled 5,000 to 6,000 gallons of cooling fluid
items.summary: Tom's Hardware reported Nov. 18 that the Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality was involved after 5,000 to 6,000 gallons of propylene glycol, a heat-transfer fluid, spilled at a SpaceXAI facility in Southaven. Tom's Hardware said the fluid reached a drainage ditch, that the department told residents there is no immediate threat to health or safety, and that the spill did not reach Horn Lake Creek. Tom's Hardware said water samples will be collected while workers clean the area. It also said a judge earlier this month rejected SpaceXAI's attempt to classify 27 gas turbines at the site as mobile units in an April 2026 pollution lawsuit.

items.headline: Tom's Hardware: a Harvard-led study puts 403 U.S. hyperscale sites at about 82 TWh
items.summary: Tom's Hardware reported Nov. 17, citing Wired, that a Harvard-led study estimates 403 hyperscale U.S. data-center sites consumed about 82 terawatt-hours in a year, 1.8 percent of U.S. electricity, compared with 99 terawatt-hours sold in Michigan in 2024. Tom's Hardware said the estimate multiplies each site's maximum capacity by the hours in a year and an assumed utilization, and that the study confirmed 403 of 675 candidate sites with satellite imagery. It said 142 of the sites are in Virginia and account for 21.4 terawatt-hours, and that an estimated 53.9 percent of the electricity came from fossil fuels, producing about 25.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide. Lead author Gianluca Guidi said the study window ended in April 2025 and the footprint could already be substantially larger.

items.headline: Tom's Hardware: manufacturers open war rooms to buy DRAM in tiny lots
items.summary: Tom's Hardware reported Nov. 26, citing The Wall Street Journal, that electronics makers, especially smaller ones, have set up procurement war rooms to find DRAM, including on eBay, and that some are buying batches of five or 12 units. Tom's Hardware said Apacer president Gibson Chen told The Wall Street Journal the company took out loans so it could pay immediately if chips appeared, and quoted him saying, "If chips show up, we take it." Tom's Hardware said Micron, Samsung, and SK hynix have shifted production toward high-bandwidth memory, that SK hynix has called 2027 the worst year for the shortage, and that new factories from the three manufacturers are not expected to start producing memory chips until 2028.
